{{Short description|How many different types are in a dataset}}
A '''diversity index''' is a method of measuring how many different types (e.g. [[species]]) there are in a dataset (e.g. a community). Diversity indices are statistical representations of different aspects of biodiversity (e.g. [[Species richness|richness]], [[Species evenness|evenness]], and [[Dominance (ecology)|dominance]]), which are useful simplifications for comparing different communities or sites.

When diversity indices are used in [[ecology]], the types of interest are usually species, but they can also be other categories, such as [[Genus|genera]], [[Family (taxonomy)|families]], [[Plant functional type|functional types]], or [[haplotype]]s. The entities of interest are usually individual organisms (e.g. plants or animals), and the measure of abundance can be, for example, number of individuals, biomass or coverage. In [[demography]], the entities of interest can be people, and the types of interest various demographic groups. In [[information science]], the entities can be characters and the types of the different letters of the alphabet. The most commonly used diversity indices are simple transformations of the effective number of types (also known as 'true diversity'), but each diversity index can also be interpreted in its own right as a measure corresponding to some real phenomenon (but a different one for each diversity index).<ref name="Hill1973">{{cite journal | last1 = Hill | first1 = M. O. | year = 1973 | title = Diversity and evenness: a unifying notation and its consequences | journal = [[Ecology (journal)|Ecology]] | volume = 54 | issue = 2| pages = 427–432 | doi = 10.2307/1934352 | jstor = 1934352 | bibcode = 1973Ecol...54..427H }}</ref><ref name="Jost2006">{{cite journal | last1 = Jost | first1 = L | year = 2006 | title = Entropy and diversity | journal = Oikos | volume = 113 | issue = 2| pages = 363–375 | doi = 10.1111/j.2006.0030-1299.14714.x | bibcode = 2006Oikos.113..363J }}</ref><ref name="Tuomisto2010a">{{cite journal | last1 = Tuomisto | first1 = H | year = 2010 | title = A diversity of beta diversities: straightening up a concept gone awry. Part 1. Defining beta diversity as a function of alpha and gamma diversity | journal = [[Ecography]] | volume = 33 | issue = 1 | pages = 2–22 | doi = 10.1111/j.1600-0587.2009.05880.x | bibcode = 2010Ecogr..33....2T }}</ref><ref name="Tuomisto2010c">{{cite journal | last1 = Tuomisto | first1 = H | year = 2010 | title = A consistent terminology for quantifying species diversity? Yes, it does exist | journal = [[Oecologia]] | volume = 164 | issue = 4| pages = 853–860 | doi = 10.1007/s00442-010-1812-0 | pmid = 20978798 | bibcode = 2010Oecol.164..853T | s2cid = 19902787 }}</ref>

Many indices only account for categorical diversity between subjects or entities. Such indices, however do not account for the [[total variation]] (diversity) that can be held between subjects or entities which occurs only when both categorical and qualitative diversity are calculated.

Diversity indices described in this article include:

* Richness, simply a count of the number of types in a dataset.
* Shannon index, which also takes into account the proportional abundance of each class under a weighted geometric mean.
** The Rényi entropy, which adds the ability to freely vary the kind of weighted mean used.
* Simpson index, which too takes into account the proportional abundance of each class under a weighted arithmetic mean
* Berger–Parker index, which gives the proportional abundance of the most abundant type.
* Effective number of species (true diversity), which allows for freely varying the kind of weighted mean used, and has a intuitive meaning.<ref name="Tuomisto2010c"/>

Some more sophisticated indices also account for the [[Phylogenetics|phylogenetic]] relatedness among the types. These are called phylo-divergence indices, and are not yet described in this article.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Tucker|first1=Caroline M.|last2=Cadotte|first2=Marc W.|last3=Carvalho|first3=Silvia B.|last4=Davies|first4=T. Jonathan|last5=Ferrier|first5=Simon|last6=Fritz|first6=Susanne A.|last7=Grenyer|first7=Rich|last8=Helmus|first8=Matthew R.|last9=Jin|first9=Lanna S.|date=May 2017|title=A guide to phylogenetic metrics for conservation, community ecology and macroecology: A guide to phylogenetic metrics for ecology|journal=Biological Reviews|volume=92|issue=2|pages=698–715|doi=10.1111/brv.12252|pmc=5096690|pmid=26785932}}</ref>

== Effective number of species or Hill numbers ==
True diversity, or the effective number of types, refers to the number of equally abundant types needed for the average proportional abundance of the types to equal that observed in the dataset of interest (where all types may not be equally abundant). The true diversity in a dataset is calculated by first taking the weighted [[generalized mean]] {{math|''M''<sub>''q''−1</sub>}} of the proportional abundances of the types in the dataset, and then taking the [[Multiplicative inverse|reciprocal]] of this. The equation is:<ref name="Tuomisto2010a" /><ref name="Tuomisto2010c" />

<math display="block">{}^q\!D = {1 \over M_{q-1}} = {1 \over \sqrt[q-1]{{\sum_{i=1}^R p_i p_i^{q-1}}}} = \left ( {\sum_{i=1}^R p_i^q} \right )^{1/(1-q)}</math>

The [[Fraction (mathematics)|denominator]] {{math|''M''<sub>''q''−1</sub>}} equals the average proportional abundance of the types in the dataset as calculated with the weighted [[generalized mean]] with exponent {{math|''q''&nbsp;−&nbsp;1}}. In the equation, {{math|''R''}} is richness (the total number of types in the dataset), and the proportional abundance of the {{math|''i''}}th type is {{math|''p''<sub>''i''</sub>}}. The proportional abundances themselves are used as the nominal weights. The numbers <math>^q D</math> are called '''Hill numbers of order''' ''q'' or '''effective number of species'''.<ref>{{Citation|last1=Chao|first1=Anne|chapter=Phylogenetic Diversity Measures and Their Decomposition: A Framework Based on Hill Numbers|date=2016|title=Biodiversity Conservation and Phylogenetic Systematics|pages=141–172|publisher=Springer International Publishing|isbn=978-3-319-22460-2|last2=Chiu|first2=Chun-Huo|last3=Jost|first3=Lou|series=Topics in Biodiversity and Conservation |volume=14 |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-22461-9_8|doi-access=free}}</ref>

When {{math|''q'' {{=}} 1}}, the above equation is undefined.  However, the [[Limit (mathematics)|mathematical limit]] as {{math|''q''}} approaches 1 is well defined and the corresponding diversity is calculated with the following equation:

<math display="block">{}^1\!D={1 \over {\prod_{i=1}^R p_i^{p_i}}} = \exp\left(-\sum_{i=1}^R p_i \ln(p_i)\right)</math>

which is the exponential of the [[Shannon entropy]] calculated with natural logarithms (see above). In other domains, this statistic is also known as the ''[[perplexity]]''.

The general equation of diversity is often written in the form<ref name="Hill1973" /><ref name="Jost2006" />

<math display="block">{}^q\!D = \left ( {\sum_{i=1}^R p_i^q} \right )^{1/(1-q)}</math>

and the term inside the parentheses is called the basic sum. Some popular diversity indices correspond to the basic sum as calculated with different values of {{math|''q''}}.<ref name="Jost2006" />

== Sensitivity of the diversity value to rare vs. abundant species ==
The value of {{math|''q''}} is often referred to as the order of the diversity. It defines the sensitivity of the true diversity to rare vs. abundant species by modifying how the weighted mean of the species' proportional abundances is calculated. With some values of the parameter {{math|''q''}}, the value of the generalized mean {{math|''M''<sub>''q''−1</sub>}} assumes familiar kinds of weighted means as special cases. In particular,

* {{math|''q'' {{=}} 0}} corresponds to the weighted [[harmonic mean]], 
* {{math|''q'' {{=}} 1}} to the weighted [[geometric mean]], and 
* {{math|''q'' {{=}} 2}} to the weighted [[arithmetic mean]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Roswell |first1=Michael |title=A conceptual guide to measuring species diversity |journal=Oikos |date=March 2021 |volume=130 |issue=3 |pages=321–338 |doi=10.1111/oik.07202 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2021Oikos.130..321R }}</ref>
* As {{math|''q''}} approaches [[infinity]], the weighted generalized mean with exponent {{math|''q''&nbsp;−&nbsp;1}} approaches the maximum {{math|''p''<sub>''i''</sub>}} value, which is the proportional abundance of the most abundant species in the dataset.

Generally, increasing the value of {{math|''q''}} increases the effective weight given to the most abundant species. This leads to obtaining a larger {{math|''M''<sub>''q''−1</sub>}} value and a smaller true diversity ({{math|''<sup>q</sup>D''}}) value with increasing {{math|''q''}}.

When {{math|''q'' {{=}} 1}}, the weighted geometric mean of the {{math|''p''<sub>''i''</sub>}} values is used, and each species is exactly weighted by its proportional abundance (in the weighted geometric mean, the weights are the exponents). When {{math|''q'' > 1}}, the weight given to abundant species is exaggerated, and when {{math|''q'' < 1}}, the weight given to rare species is. At {{math|''q'' {{=}} 0}}, the species weights exactly cancel out the species proportional abundances, such that the weighted mean of the {{math|''p''<sub>''i''</sub>}} values equals {{math|1 / ''R''}} even when all species are not equally abundant. At {{math|''q'' {{=}} 0}}, the effective number of species, {{math|<sup>0</sup>''D''}}, hence equals the actual number of species {{math|''R''}}. In the context of diversity, {{math|''q''}} is generally limited to non-negative values. This is because negative values of {{math|''q''}} would give rare species so much more weight than abundant ones that {{math|<sup>''q''</sup>''D''}} would exceed {{math|''R''}}.<ref name="Tuomisto2010a" /><ref name="Tuomisto2010c" />

==Richness==
{{main|Species richness}}
Richness {{math|''R''}} simply quantifies how many different types the dataset of interest contains. For example, species richness (usually noted {{math|''S''}}) is simply the number of species, e.g. at a particular site. Richness is a simple measure, so it has been a popular diversity index in ecology, where abundance data are often not available.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Morris |first1=E. Kathryn |last2=Caruso |first2=Tancredi |last3=Buscot |first3=François |last4=Fischer |first4=Markus |last5=Hancock |first5=Christine |last6=Maier |first6=Tanja S. |last7=Meiners |first7=Torsten |last8=Müller |first8=Caroline |last9=Obermaier |first9=Elisabeth |last10=Prati |first10=Daniel |last11=Socher |first11=Stephanie A. |last12=Sonnemann |first12=Ilja |last13=Wäschke |first13=Nicole |last14=Wubet |first14=Tesfaye |last15=Wurst |first15=Susanne |date=September 2014 |title=Choosing and using diversity indices: insights for ecological applications from the German Biodiversity Exploratories |journal=Ecology and Evolution |language=en |volume=4 |issue=18 |pages=3514–3524 |doi=10.1002/ece3.1155 |doi-access=free |issn=2045-7758 |pmc=4224527 |pmid=25478144|bibcode=2014EcoEv...4.3514M }}</ref> If true diversity is calculated with {{math|''q'' {{=}} 0}}, the effective number of types ({{math|<sup>0</sup>''D''}}) equals the actual number of types, which is identical to Richness ({{math|''R''}}).<ref name=Jost2006 /><ref name=Tuomisto2010c />

==<span class="anchor" id="Shannon index"></span>Shannon index==
The '''Shannon index''' has been a popular diversity index in the ecological literature, where it is also known as '''Shannon's diversity index''', '''Shannon–[[Norbert Wiener|Wiener]] index''', and (erroneously) '''Shannon–[[Warren Weaver|Weaver]] index'''.<ref name=Spellerberg2003>Spellerberg, Ian F., and Peter J. Fedor. (2003) A tribute to Claude Shannon (1916–2001) and a plea for more rigorous use of species richness, species diversity and the 'Shannon–Wiener'Index. [[Global Ecology and Biogeography]] 12.3, 177-179.</ref> The measure was originally proposed by [[Claude Shannon]] in 1948 to quantify the [[Entropy (information theory)|entropy]] (hence ''Shannon entropy'', related to [[Shannon information content]]) in strings of text.<ref name=Shannon1948>Shannon, C. E. (1948) [[A mathematical theory of communication]].  The Bell System Technical Journal, 27, 379–423 and 623–656.</ref> The idea is that the more letters there are, and the closer their proportional abundances in the string of interest, the more difficult it is to correctly predict which letter will be the next one in the string. The Shannon entropy quantifies the uncertainty (entropy or degree of surprise) associated with this prediction. It is most often calculated as follows:

<math display="block"> H' = -\sum_{i=1}^R p_i \ln(p_i) </math>

where {{math|''p''<sub>''i''</sub>}} is the proportion of characters belonging to the {{math|''i''}}th type of letter in the string of interest. In ecology, {{math|''p''<sub>''i''</sub>}} is often the proportion of individuals belonging to the {{math|''i''}}th species in the dataset of interest. Then the Shannon entropy quantifies the uncertainty in predicting the species identity of an individual that is taken at random from the dataset.

Although the equation is here written with natural [[logarithm]]s, the base of the logarithm used when calculating the Shannon entropy can be chosen freely. Shannon himself discussed logarithm bases 2, 10 and {{math|''e''}}, and these have since become the most popular bases in applications that use the Shannon entropy. Each log base corresponds to a different measurement unit, which has been called binary digits (bits), decimal digits (decits), and natural digits (nats) for the bases 2, 10 and {{math|''e''}}, respectively. Comparing Shannon entropy values that were originally calculated with different log bases requires converting them to the same log base: change from the base {{math|''a''}} to base {{math|''b''}} is obtained with multiplication by {{math|log<sub>''b''</sub>''(a)''}}.<ref name=Shannon1948 />

The Shannon index ({{math|''H'''}}) is related to the [[weighted geometric mean]] of the proportional abundances of the types. Specifically, it equals the logarithm of true diversity as calculated with {{math|''q'' {{=}} 1}}:<ref name=Tuomisto2010a />

<math display="block"> H' = -\sum_{i=1}^R p_i \ln(p_i) = -\sum_{i=1}^R \ln\left(p_i^{p_i}\right)</math>

This can also be written

<math display="block">\begin{align}
 H' &= -\left[\ln\left(p_1^{p_1}\right) +\ln\left(p_2^{p_2}\right) +\ln\left(p_3^{p_3}\right) + \cdots + \ln\left(p_R^{p_R}\right)\right] \\[1ex]
 &= -\ln\left(p_1^{p_1}p_2^{p_2}p_3^{p_3} \cdots p_R^{p_R}\right)
 = \ln \left ( {1 \over p_1^{p_1}p_2^{p_2}p_3^{p_3} \cdots p_R^{p_R}} \right ) \\
 &= \ln \left ( {1 \over {\prod_{i=1}^R p_i^{p_i}}} \right )
\end{align}</math>

Since the sum of the {{math|''p''<sub>''i''</sub>}} values equals 1 by definition, the [[denominator]] equals the weighted geometric mean of the {{math|''p''<sub>''i''</sub>}} values, with the {{math|''p''<sub>''i''</sub>}} values themselves being used as the weights (exponents in the equation). The term within the parentheses hence equals true diversity {{math|<sup>1</sup>''D''}}, and {{math|''H'''}} equals {{math|ln(<sup>1</sup>''D'')}}.<ref name=Hill1973 /><ref name=Tuomisto2010a /><ref name=Tuomisto2010c />

When all types in the dataset of interest are equally common, all {{math|''p''<sub>''i''</sub>}} values equal {{math|1 / ''R''}}, and the Shannon index hence takes the value {{math|ln(''R'')}}. The more unequal the abundances of the types, the larger the weighted geometric mean of the {{math|''p''<sub>''i''</sub>}} values, and the smaller the corresponding Shannon entropy. If practically all abundance is concentrated to one type, and the other types are very rare (even if there are many of them), Shannon entropy approaches zero. When there is only one type in the dataset, Shannon entropy exactly equals zero (there is no uncertainty in predicting the type of the next randomly chosen entity).

In machine learning the Shannon index is also called as [[Decision tree learning#Information gain|Information gain]].

===Rényi entropy===
The [[Rényi entropy]] is a generalization of the Shannon entropy to other values of {{math|''q''}} than 1. It can be expressed:

<math display="block">{}^qH = \frac{1}{1-q} \; \ln\left ( \sum_{i=1}^R p_i^q \right ) </math>

which equals

<math display="block">{}^qH = \ln\left ( {1 \over \sqrt[q-1]{{\sum_{i=1}^R p_i p_i^{q-1}}}} \right ) = \ln({}^q\!D)</math>

This means that taking the logarithm of true diversity based on any value of {{math|''q''}} gives the Rényi entropy corresponding to the same value of {{math|''q''}}.

==Simpson index==
The Simpson index was introduced in 1949 by [[Edward H. Simpson]] to measure the degree of concentration when individuals are classified into types.<ref name=Simpson1949>{{cite journal | last1 = Simpson | first1 = E. H. | year = 1949 | title = Measurement of diversity | journal = Nature | volume = 163 | issue = 4148| page = 688 | doi=10.1038/163688a0| bibcode = 1949Natur.163..688S | doi-access = free }}</ref> The same index was rediscovered by [[Orris C. Herfindahl]] in 1950.<ref>Herfindahl, O. C. (1950) Concentration in the U.S. Steel Industry. Unpublished doctoral dissertation, Columbia University.</ref> The square root of the index had already been introduced in 1945 by the economist [[Albert O. Hirschman]].<ref>Hirschman, A. O. (1945) National power and the structure of foreign trade. Berkeley.</ref> As a result, the same measure is usually known as the Simpson index in ecology, and as the [[Herfindahl index]] or the Herfindahl–Hirschman index (HHI) in economics.

The measure equals the probability that two entities taken at random from the dataset of interest represent the same type.<ref name=Simpson1949 /> It equals:

<math display="block"> \lambda = \sum_{i=1}^R p_i^2,</math>

where {{math|''R''}} is richness (the total number of types in the dataset). This equation is also equal to the weighted arithmetic mean of the proportional abundances {{math|''p''<sub>''i''</sub>}} of the types of interest, with the proportional abundances themselves being used as the weights.<ref name=Hill1973 /> Proportional abundances are by definition constrained to values between zero and one, but it is a weighted arithmetic mean, hence {{math|''λ'' ≥ 1/''R''}}, which is reached when all types are equally abundant.

By comparing the equation used to calculate λ with the equations used to calculate true diversity, it can be seen that {{math|1/λ}} equals {{math|<sup>2</sup>''D''}}, i.e., true diversity as calculated with {{math|''q'' {{=}} 2}}. The original Simpson's index hence equals the corresponding basic sum.<ref name=Jost2006 />

The interpretation of λ as the probability that two entities taken at random from the dataset of interest represent the same type assumes that the entities are sampled with replacement. If the dataset is very large, sampling without replacement gives approximately the same result, but in small datasets, the difference can be substantial. If the dataset is small, and sampling without replacement is assumed, the probability of obtaining the same type with both random draws is:

<math display="block"> \ell = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^R n_i (n_i -1)}{N (N-1)} </math>

where {{math|''n''<sub>''i''</sub>}} is the number of entities belonging to the {{math|''i''}}th type and {{math|''N''}} is the total number of entities in the dataset.<ref name=Simpson1949 /> This form of the Simpson index is also known as the Hunter–Gaston index in microbiology.<ref name=Hunter1988>{{cite journal|last1=Hunter|first1=PR|last2=Gaston|first2=MA|year=1988|title=Numerical index of the discriminatory ability of typing systems: an application of Simpson's index of diversity|volume=26|issue=11|pages=2465–2466|pmid=3069867|journal=J Clin Microbiol|doi=10.1128/JCM.26.11.2465-2466.1988|pmc=266921 |bibcode=1988JCMb...26.2465H }}</ref>

Since the mean proportional abundance of the types increases with decreasing number of types and increasing abundance of the most abundant type, λ obtains small values in datasets of high diversity and large values in datasets of low diversity. This is counterintuitive behavior for a diversity index, so often, such transformations of λ that increase with increasing diversity have been used instead. The most popular of such indices have been the inverse Simpson index (1/λ) and the [[Corrado Gini|Gini]]–Simpson index (1&nbsp;−&nbsp;λ).<ref name=Hill1973 /><ref name=Jost2006 /> Both of these have also been called the Simpson index in the ecological literature, so care is needed to avoid accidentally comparing the different indices as if they were the same.

===Inverse Simpson index===
The inverse Simpson index equals:

<math display="block"> \frac 1 \lambda = {1 \over\sum_{i=1}^R p_i^2} = {}^2D</math>

This simply equals true diversity of order 2, i.e. the effective number of types that is obtained when the weighted arithmetic mean is used to quantify average proportional abundance of types in the dataset of interest.

The index is also used as a measure of the [[effective number of parties]].

===Gini–Simpson index===

The Gini-Simpson Index is also called [[Decision tree learning#Gini impurity|Gini impurity]], or '''Gini's diversity index'''<ref>{{cite web |title=Growing Decision Trees |url=https://www.mathworks.com/help/stats/growing-decision-trees.html |website=MathWorks }}</ref> in the field of [[machine learning]]. The original Simpson index λ equals the probability that two entities taken at random from the dataset of interest (with replacement) represent the same type. Its transformation 1&nbsp;−&nbsp;λ, therefore, equals the probability that the two entities represent different types. This measure is also known in ecology as the probability of interspecific encounter (''PIE'')<ref>{{cite journal|author=Hurlbert, S.H.|year=1971|title=The nonconcept of species diversity: A critique and alternative parameters|journal=[[Ecology (journal)|Ecology]]|volume=52|issue=4|pages=577–586|doi=10.2307/1934145|pmid=28973811|jstor=1934145|bibcode=1971Ecol...52..577H |s2cid=25837001 }}</ref> and the Gini–Simpson index.<ref name=Jost2006 /> It can be expressed as a transformation of the true diversity of order 2:

<math display="block"> 1 - \lambda = 1 - \sum_{i=1}^R p_i^2 = 1 - \frac{1}{{}^2D}</math>

The Gibbs–Martin index of sociology, psychology, and management studies,<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Gibbs, Jack P. |author2=William T. Martin|year=1962|title=Urbanization, technology and the division of labor|journal=[[American Sociological Review]]|volume=27|issue=5|pages=667–677|jstor=2089624|doi=10.2307/2089624}}</ref> which is also known as the Blau index, is the same measure as the Gini–Simpson index.

The quantity is also known as the [[Zygosity#Heterozygosity in population genetics|expected heterozygosity]] in [[population genetics]].

==Berger–Parker index==
The Berger–Parker index, named after [[Wolfgang H. Berger]] and [[Frances Lawrence Parker]],<ref>{{cite journal|journal=[[Science (journal)|Science]]|date=June 1970|volume=168|issue=3937|pages=1345–1347|doi=10.1126/science.168.3937.1345|title=Diversity of Planktonic Foraminifera in Deep-Sea Sediments|first1=Wolfgang H.|last1=Berger|first2=Frances L.|last2=Parker|pmid=17731043|bibcode=1970Sci...168.1345B|s2cid=29553922 }}</ref> equals the maximum {{math|''p''<sub>''i''</sub>}} value in the dataset, i.e., the proportional abundance of the most abundant type. This corresponds to the weighted [[generalized mean]] of the {{math|''p''<sub>''i''</sub>}} values when {{math|''q''}} approaches infinity, and hence equals the inverse of the true diversity of order infinity ({{math|1/<sup>∞</sup>''D''}}).
